summary: Older, highly effective MAOI antidepressant used for hard-to-treat depression. Not a first-line option because food and drug interactions can trigger dangerous blood pressure spikes.
description: Tranylcypromine (Parnate) is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) used for adults with major depression who haven’t responded to other antidepressants. It can work well, especially in severe or treatment-resistant cases—but it comes with strict rules. Mixing it with certain meds or high-tyramine foods (like aged cheeses and cured meats) can trigger a hypertensive crisis, which can be fatal. It can also cause dizziness when standing, insomnia, agitation, and (rarely) serotonin syndrome. If you take it, you need a clear food list, a clean medication list, and a plan for safe switches and tapering.
patient_summary: Parnate can be a game-changer for treatment-resistant depression, but it’s not “set it and forget it.” You have to follow the MAOI food rules and avoid a long list of interacting meds. The biggest danger is a hypertensive crisis from tyramine foods or certain drugs—so you’ll need blood pressure monitoring, a strict interaction check, and careful washout periods when switching antidepressants.

primary.context: Used for adults with major depression who have not improved enough with other antidepressants. Typically reserved for treatment-resistant depression because of interaction risk and dietary restrictions.

therapeutic_response.display: Depression: initial effects may appear within 1 to 2 weeks; continued improvement through 4 to 6 weeks

common_adverse_effects.notes: Feeling lightheaded when you stand up can happen, especially above 30 mg/day or during dose increases. Hydration and slow position changes help, but persistent dizziness or fainting needs medical attention.
Parnate can be activating. Some people feel more energy, but others feel restless, jittery, or unable to sleep—especially early on. Dose timing and slower titration can reduce this.
Activation can look like anxiety, agitation, irritability, or pacing. If it feels intense, escalating, or comes with suicidal thoughts, call your clinician immediately.
Headaches can be a routine side effect, but with MAOIs you can’t ignore them. Sudden severe headache—especially with sweating, palpitations, nausea, or neck stiffness—can signal hypertensive crisis.

common_adverse_effects.effect: GI effects (nausea, constipation, diarrhea, abdominal pain) and dry mouth
common_adverse_effects.notes: Dry mouth and constipation are common nuisance effects. Nausea can happen early and may improve with time.
Heart racing can occur. If it’s new, severe, or paired with headache or chest pain, treat it seriously and get evaluated.

serious_risks.risk: Hypertensive crisis (sometimes fatal): severe headache (often occipital), nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, sweating, photophobia, palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, seizures—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Intracranial bleeding reported in association with severe blood pressure elevation—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.

Serotonin syndrome (especially with serotonergic meds or other MAO inhibitors): agitation, hallucinations, delirium, fever, sweating, tremor, rigidity, myoclonus, diarrhea, seizures—MEDICAL EMERGENCY.
Mania/hypomania: decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsivity, risky behavior, irritability—requires urgent clinical reassessment.
SIADH (low sodium): confusion, weakness, headache, nausea—requires medical evaluation.
Blood dyscrasias (rare): agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia—seek care for fever, sore throat, unusual bruising/bleeding.
Hepatitis/elevated liver enzymes (reported): jaundice, dark urine, right upper abdominal pain—stop and seek care.

safety.black_box_warning: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening, and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Tranylcypromine is not approved for use in pediatric patients.

contraindications.contraindication: Pheochromocytoma or other catecholamine-releasing paragangliomas (hypertensive crisis risk)
Concurrent use or use in rapid succession with other antidepressants (including SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, other MAOIs, and many others listed in labeling)
Concurrent use with sympathomimetic agents (eg, pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine, ephedrine; stimulants and related products)
Concurrent use with certain dopaminergic/serotonergic agents (eg, levodopa, tryptophan, SAM-e, hydroxytryptophan) and other listed interacting agents
Use with high-tyramine foods/beverages (hypertensive crisis risk)

precautions: Hypertensive crisis can occur (sometimes fatal), especially with high-tyramine foods/beverages or interacting medications—even after stopping, risk may persist up to 10 days
Serotonin syndrome can occur if combined with serotonergic agents or other MAO inhibitors (including certain non-psychiatric MAO inhibitors like linezolid or IV methylene blue)
Orthostatic hypotension and fainting can occur, especially at doses >30 mg/day
CNS depression can impair driving, operating machinery, and decision-making
Can trigger mania or hypomania in people with bipolar vulnerability—screen before starting
Seizure risk: reported with overdose and with withdrawal after misuse/abuse

interactions.interactant: High-tyramine foods and beverages (aged/mature cheeses, cured meats, draft/tap beer, Marmite/yeast extracts, sauerkraut, soy sauce and fermented soy condiments, fava/broad bean pods; and especially spoiled/improperly stored foods)
interactions.mechanism: Hypertensive crisis: sudden, severe blood pressure elevation that can be fatal or cause stroke/intracranial bleeding.
interactions.action: Avoid tyramine-rich foods and beverages during treatment and for at least 2 weeks after stopping. Freshness matters—avoid questionable leftovers or spoiled foods. If severe headache, sweating, palpitations, chest pain, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, or shortness of breath occurs: emergency evaluation.

interactions.interactant: Other antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, other MAOIs, and many atypicals including agents like bupropion, trazodone, vilazodone, vortioxetine, etc.)
interactions.mechanism: Serotonin syndrome and/or hypertensive reactions; potentially life-threatening.
interactions.action: Do not combine. Use washout periods when switching (see Switching/Washout in Tapering section).

interactions.interactant: Sympathomimetics and stimulants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine, ephedrine; amphetamines and methylphenidate products; many weight-loss/energy supplements)
interactions.mechanism: Hypertensive crisis and dangerous cardiovascular effects.
interactions.action: Avoid. This includes many OTC cold/flu medications. Check every OTC label and ask before taking anything.
Avoid entirely while on Parnate and during washout.

interactions.mechanism: Severe reaction including serotonin syndrome-like toxicity; can be fatal.
interactions.action: Contraindicated. Tell any ER/surgical team you take an MAOI.

interactions.interactant: Triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, buspirone, St John’s wort, tryptophan and related serotonergic supplements (and other serotonergic agents)
interactions.action: Avoid combination unless a specialist explicitly manages it (and in many cases it remains contraindicated).

interactions.interactant: Caffeine and certain amino-acid related triggers (tyrosine, phenylalanine, dopamine-related products; tryptophan supplements)
interactions.mechanism: Can contribute to sudden severe blood pressure elevation and/or toxicity in susceptible situations.
interactions.action: Keep caffeine modest and consistent; avoid supplement stacks and amino-acid boosters. If you’re not sure what’s in it, don’t take it.
Monitor blood glucose closely when starting or adjusting doses.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Blood pressure and heart rate: baseline and regularly during treatment and dose changes; urgent evaluation for severe headache, palpitations, chest pain, sweating, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, shortness of breath, or neurologic symptoms.

Mental status and mood: worsening depression, emergent suicidality, agitation, irritability, insomnia, panic symptoms, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania/mania—especially during the first 1 to 2 months and during dose increases/decreases.
Food/diet adherence: review tyramine restrictions and reinforce freshness rules; assess for accidental exposures.
Medication reconciliation: every visit (and before any new prescription/OTC/supplement) because interaction risk is high and can be life-threatening.
Blood glucose: in patients with diabetes or those using insulin/oral hypoglycemics due to hypoglycemia risk.
Hepatic and renal function: baseline and periodically in higher-risk patients; use caution in hepatic impairment.
Adverse effects that increase risk: orthostatic hypotension (falls/syncope), insomnia/activation, agitation, tremor/myoclonus, and any signs consistent with serotonin syndrome.

special_populations.pregnancy: Human data are limited. If pregnant (or trying), this requires a risk-benefit conversation that includes depression severity, past response to other medications, and non-medication options. If exposure occurs during pregnancy, consider enrollment in the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants (NPRAD) (844-405-6185).
special_populations.lactation: Tranylcypromine is present in breast milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the nursing infant, the manufacturer recommends deciding whether to discontinue breastfeeding or discontinue the medication, based on the importance of treatment to the mother.
special_populations.pediatric: Not approved for pediatric patients. Antidepressants increase risk of suicidal thinking/behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults; tranylcypromine is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
special_populations.geriatric: Refer to adult dosing, but start lower and increase more gradually. Older adults may be more prone to orthostatic hypotension, falls, and medication interaction complications.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No dosage adjustments are provided in manufacturer labeling.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No specific dose adjustments are provided in manufacturer labeling; use with caution. Hepatitis and elevated liver enzymes have been reported—monitor clinically and consider alternatives if liver disease is significant.

pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Tyramine-containing foods/beverages can trigger severe blood pressure elevation (hypertensive crisis). Food freshness matters—spoiled or improperly stored foods can contain higher tyramine.

dosing.titration: Parnate is taken by mouth in divided doses. Dosing usually starts low and increases gradually based on response and tolerability. This is typically reserved for adults with depression that hasn’t responded to other treatments.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Stopping Parnate needs planning. MAOI effects can persist up to 10 days after discontinuation, and antidepressant discontinuation symptoms can happen—sometimes more intensely with MAOIs. Tapering also helps you see whether depression symptoms are returning.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Parnate (tranylcypromine) is an MAOI antidepressant used for {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:major depression} in adults—usually when other treatments haven’t worked well enough. It can be extremely effective, but it requires strict food and medication rules to avoid dangerous interactions.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (unipolar)}: For adults who have not responded adequately to other antidepressants
Treatment-resistant depression: When multiple first-line antidepressants and/or therapy haven’t been enough

After a couple weeks, I noticed I could get out of bed without negotiating with my brain for an hour.

I had to take hydration seriously.
The food rules made me anxious at first, but once I had a list, it was manageable.

sections.intro: People’s experiences vary a lot with MAOIs. Here are the patterns that come up most often:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Parnate doesn’t work like a PRN anxiety med. It’s a daily antidepressant that builds over time—but MAOI enzyme effects can stick around even after the pills stop.
key_points: 1-2 weeks: Some people notice early changes (energy, sleep, emotional reactivity)
4-6 weeks: More complete antidepressant effect often becomes clearer
1.5 hours: Approximate time to peak serum levels
2.5 hours: Approximate elimination half-life (but this does NOT reflect how long MAOI effects can last)
Up to 10 days after stopping: MAO inhibition can persist, which is why washout periods matter

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Parnate is often reserved for depression that hasn’t improved with other antidepressants. In real-world practice, it can be highly effective for the right patient—especially when the depression is severe and persistent. The tradeoff is safety: the effectiveness comes with strict interaction rules and a bigger monitoring burden.
sections.clinical_details: This medication’s value is less about a single headline number and more about its role as a later-line option when standard SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs and therapy haven’t been enough. Clinicians choose it when potential benefit justifies the higher interaction risk and required dietary restrictions.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: This is an MAOI: food and medication interactions can be dangerous. Hypertensive crisis is the emergency to know.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening, and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Tranylcypromine is not approved for use in pediatric patients.

Orthostatic hypotension and fainting can occur, especially at doses >30 mg/day
CNS depression can impair driving, operating machinery, and decision-making
Can trigger mania or hypomania in people with bipolar vulnerability—screen before starting
Seizure risk: reported with overdose and with withdrawal after misuse/abuse
patient_counseling: Get a written MAOI food list and keep it on your phone. When in doubt, skip the food and ask.
Avoid high-tyramine foods and beverages (aged cheeses, cured meats, draft beer, certain fermented/soy products). Freshness matters—spoiled or improperly stored foods can be riskier.
Tell every clinician (including dentists, urgent care, ER) that you take an MAOI. This changes what meds are safe.
Monitor blood pressure as instructed—especially during titration and if you get headaches, palpitations, chest tightness, sweating, or nausea.

Know hypertensive crisis warning signs: severe headache (often in the back of the head), stiff/sore neck, nausea/vomiting, sweating, photophobia, chest pain, shortness of breath, seizures—this is an emergency.
If mood becomes unusually energized, impulsive, irritable, sleepless, or 'too good,' call your prescriber—this can be hypomania/mania.

During the first 1-2 months (and during dose changes), monitor for worsening depression, agitation, insomnia, panic symptoms, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, or suicidal thoughts—tell your clinician immediately.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Common themes: activation (agitation, insomnia), blood pressure effects (orthostatic hypotension), and anticholinergic-ish symptoms (dry mouth, constipation). Rare but serious risks include hypertensive crisis, serotonin syndrome (with interactions), and mood switching into mania.
plain_language_list: Dizziness when standing (orthostatic hypotension) and sometimes fainting
Insomnia or feeling 'wired' (especially early or after dose increases)
Sexual side effects (difficulty orgasm, erectile/ejaculatory issues)

sections.intro: With Parnate, interactions are the whole game. The two big nightmares are hypertensive crisis (from tyramine or sympathomimetics) and serotonin syndrome (from serotonergic drugs). Also: MAOI effects can persist up to ~10 days after stopping, so interactions can still happen during that window.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stopping Parnate needs planning. MAOI effects can persist up to 10 days after discontinuation, and antidepressant discontinuation symptoms can happen—sometimes more intensely with MAOIs. Tapering also helps you see whether depression symptoms are returning.
key_points: If treated ≥4 weeks: taper gradually over ~2 to 4 weeks to reduce withdrawal symptoms and to detect relapse early.
If treated 2 to 3 weeks: taper may be done over ~1 to 2 weeks.
If treated <2 weeks: taper often isn’t required, but some people are sensitive—clinician judgment matters.
Consider slower tapers (≥4 weeks) if you’ve had withdrawal symptoms before or you were on higher doses.
Some people on long-term treatment (>6 months), especially with a history of discontinuation syndrome, may benefit from very slow tapers (sometimes >3 months).
If withdrawal becomes intolerable: go back to the prior dose and taper more slowly.
Washout matters: MAOI effects can persist up to ~10 days after stopping, so interaction risk can continue even when you’re no longer taking pills.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Parnate is taken by mouth in divided doses. Dosing usually starts low and increases gradually based on response and tolerability. This is typically reserved for adults with depression that hasn’t responded to other treatments.

adult.mdd_initial: 10 to 30 mg/day PO in divided doses
adult.mdd_titration: If symptoms do not improve after 2 weeks, increase by 10 mg/day at 1- to 3-week intervals based on response/tolerability
adult.mdd_typical: 30 to 60 mg/day PO in divided doses

sections.simple_explanation: Because MAOIs have higher interaction risk and can affect blood pressure, clinicians usually titrate more carefully than with many newer antidepressants. The goal is the lowest effective dose that improves depression without causing intolerable side effects.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Parnate has limited pregnancy data and meaningful safety concerns related to blood pressure and interactions. It’s not approved for pediatric patients. Older adults may be more sensitive to blood pressure changes and side effects, so dosing is typically slower and more cautious.

If exposure occurs during pregnancy, consider enrollment in the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants (NPRAD) (844-405-6185).

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Parnate is available as an oral tablet. Most dosing is built from the 10 mg tablet, adjusted gradually to balance benefit and side effects.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Parnate is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI). It blocks the enzyme that breaks down key neurotransmitters—norepinephrine, serotonin, and dopamine-related signaling—so levels rise in the brain. That increase can improve depressive symptoms, but the same mechanism is why food and drug interactions can become medically dangerous.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Parnate is typically not a first-line antidepressant. It’s usually considered when someone has tried multiple standard options (like SSRIs/SNRIs and evidence-based psychotherapy) and still hasn’t improved enough. The upside is that MAOIs can work when other antidepressants fail. The downside is the higher safety burden: strict diet rules, strict interaction screening, and careful washout periods during medication changes.

faqs.a: Parnate (tranylcypromine) is used for major depressive disorder in adults—typically when other antidepressants haven’t worked well enough. It’s usually reserved for treatment-resistant depression because MAOIs require strict diet rules and have high-risk drug interactions.

faqs.q: How long does Parnate take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice early changes within 1 to 2 weeks, but fuller antidepressant effects often build over 4 to 6 weeks. Dose adjustments are usually spaced out because tolerability and blood pressure effects need monitoring.

faqs.q: Why are there food restrictions with Parnate?
faqs.a: Because it’s an MAOI. Foods high in tyramine can trigger a sudden and dangerous spike in blood pressure (hypertensive crisis). The classic examples are aged cheeses, cured meats, draft beer, and fermented/soy products—but freshness matters too: spoiled or improperly stored foods can have higher tyramine.

faqs.q: What does a hypertensive crisis feel like?
faqs.a: Often like a sudden severe headache (commonly in the back of the head), plus symptoms like sweating, nausea/vomiting, neck stiffness, palpitations, chest tightness, shortness of breath, or sensitivity to light. It can also cause seizures or neurologic symptoms. This is an emergency—seek urgent care immediately.

faqs.q: Can I take cold medicine with Parnate?
faqs.a: You have to be extremely careful. Many OTC cold and sinus meds contain sympathomimetics (like pseudoephedrine or phenylephrine), which can trigger dangerously high blood pressure with MAOIs. Don’t self-prescribe OTC meds—check labels and confirm with a pharmacist or prescriber first.

faqs.q: Can Parnate be combined with SSRIs or SNRIs?
faqs.a: No—combining MAOIs with serotonergic antidepressants can cause serotonin syndrome, which can be life-threatening. Switching requires washout periods, and fluoxetine requires a longer wait because it stays in the body longer.

faqs.q: What washout periods are needed when switching antidepressants?
faqs.a: Common rules: wait 14 days between stopping most antidepressants (without long-lasting metabolites) and starting Parnate; wait at least 5 to 6 weeks after stopping fluoxetine before starting Parnate; and after stopping Parnate, wait about 7 to 14 days before starting another antidepressant or MAOI. Your clinician may adjust timing based on the specific medication and your risk factors.

faqs.q: Can Parnate cause insomnia or agitation?
faqs.a: Yes. Parnate can feel activating—especially early in treatment or during dose increases. People may feel wired, restless, anxious, or have trouble sleeping. Dose timing and slower titration can help, but intense agitation or new suicidal thoughts need urgent follow-up.

All antidepressants carry a boxed warning: in short-term studies, they increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults (18 to 24). That’s why close monitoring matters—especially in the first 1 to 2 months and during dose changes. Tranylcypromine is not approved for pediatric patients.

It can. Like other antidepressants, it may precipitate mania or hypomania in people with bipolar vulnerability. That’s why clinicians screen for bipolar disorder before starting, and why a sudden jump into decreased sleep, racing thoughts, impulsivity, or unusually elevated mood should be reported immediately.

faqs.q: How do you stop Parnate safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been on it for several weeks, clinicians usually taper gradually over about 2 to 4 weeks to reduce discontinuation symptoms and to watch for returning depression. Some people need a slower taper. Also, MAOI effects can persist up to about 10 days after stopping, so interaction precautions still matter during that window.

seo.description: Parnate (tranylcypromine) is an MAOI for treatment-resistant depression. Learn dosing (10–60 mg/day), tyramine food restrictions, dangerous drug interactions, hypertensive crisis warning signs, serotonin syndrome risk, and tapering/washout rules.
